Operator
Good morning. My name is Rivka, and I'll be your conference facilitator today. At this time, I would like to welcome everyone to Boise Cascade's Q1 2025 Earnings Conference Call. All lines have been placed on mute to prevent any background noise. After the speaker's remarks, there will be a question and answer period. It is now my pleasure to introduce you to Chris Forrey, Vice President, Finance and Investor Relations, Boise Cascade. Mr. Forrey, you may begin your conference.
Chris Forrey
VP of Finance and Investor Relations, Boise Cascade
Thank you, Rivka, and good morning, everyone. I'd like to welcome you to Boise Cascade's Q1 2025 earnings call and business update. Joining me on today's call are Nate Jorgensen, our CEO, Jeff Strom, our COO, Kelly Hibbs, our CFO, Troy Little, head of our wood products operations, and Joe Barney, head of our building materials distribution operations.
Turning to slide two. This call will contain forward-looking statements. Please review the warning statements in our press release, on the presentation slides, and in our filings with the SEC regarding the risks associated with these forward-looking statements. Also, please note that the appendix includes reconciliations from our GAAP net income to EBITDA, and adjusted EBITDA and segment income to segment EBITDA. I will now turn the call over to Nate.
Nathan Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Thanks, Chris. Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us for our earnings call today. I'm on slide three. Total US housing starts and single-family housing starts decreased 2% and 6% respectively, compared to the prior year quarter. Our consolidated Q1 sales of $1.5 billion were down 7% from Q1 2024. Our net income was $40.3 million or $1.06 per share, compared to net income of $104.1 million or $2.61 per share in the year ago quarter. Our team delivered solid results during the quarter when considering an environment influenced by constrained demand, uncertain trade policies, and difficult weather. Home buyer affordability challenges continue to affect demand, and we were compounded by increasing economic uncertainty that has led to lower consumer and builder confidence.
Despite the backdrop, our associates across the company remain clearly focused on delivering value to our customer and vendor partners, for which I'm incredibly grateful. In addition, the plant outage at our Oakdale, Louisiana plywood and veneer facility mill negatively impacted our Q1 results. The significant modernization projects underway there are on schedule to be completed at the end of Q2 and will contribute to the ongoing strength of our EWP franchise. Lastly, our clear focus on strategic investments and returns of capital to our shareholders is bolstered by the strength of our balance sheet and our constructive view on long-term demand drivers for residential construction. Kelly will now walk through our financial segment results and provide an update on our capital allocation priorities. After which, I'll provide an outlook before we take your questions. Kelly?
Kelly Hibbs
CFO, Boise Cascade
Thank you, Nate, and good morning, everyone. Wood Products sales in Q1, including sales to our distribution segment, were $415.8 million, down 11% compared to Q1 2024. Wood Products segment EBITDA was $40.2 million, compared to EBITDA of $95.6 million reported in the year-ago quarter. The decrease in segment EBITDA was due primarily to lower EWP and plywood sales prices, and lower EWP volumes. In addition, the scheduled Oakdale outage negatively impacted year-over-year and sequential EBITDA comparisons by approximately $8 million and $7 million, respectively. In BMD, our sales in the quarter were $1.4 billion, down 7% from Q1 2024. BMD reported segment EBITDA of $62.8 million in Q1, compared to segment EBITDA of $83.6 million in the prior year quarter.
BMD's gross margin dollars decreased $20.4 million from Q1 2024, and our gross margin was 14.7%, a 40 basis points decline year-over-year. Turning to Slide five. On a year-over-year basis, Q1 volumes for both LVL and I-joist were down 3%, better than the 6% year-over-year decline in single-family housing starts. The pullback in starts stems from a consistent theme we hear from the builder community around moderating the pace of new starts as they continue to sell through higher than anticipated inventory levels. As it relates to pricing, sequential results for both LVL and I-joist were down 3% due to continued pricing pressure created by the constrained demand environment and competition for share. Turning to Slide six.
Our Q1 plywood sales volume was 363 million ft² , compared to 372 million feet in Q1 2024, primarily driven by the planned outage at our Oakdale mill. The 341 per thousand average plywood net sales price in the Q1 was down 10% on a year-over-year basis and down 3% sequentially. Moving to slides seven and eight. BMD's year-over-year Q1 sales decline of 7% was driven by a 5% decrease in volume and a 2% decrease in price. By product line, commodity sales decreased 7%, general line product sales decreased 3%, and sales of EWP decreased 13%. Weather meaningfully influenced our sales activity in the Q1, with our January and February daily pace below 21.5 million before March rebounded to exceed 24 million per day.
As I mentioned earlier, BMD's Q1 gross margin percentage was 14.7%, down 40 basis points year-over-year. In particular, gross margin dollars were affected by lower sales volumes and decreased margins on commodity and EWP products. BMD's EBITDA margin was 4.5% for the quarter, down from the 5.6% reported in the year-ago quarter, a reflection of lower gross margin dollar opportunity from slower sales activity and the associated deleveraging of our cost base. However, it is important to again reference the improved sales velocity in March, which resulted in EBITDA margins for that month similar to levels seen in recent quarters.
Our BMD team continues to consistently provide high service levels across a broad mix of best-in-class products, and as we have spoken to in the past, periods like now, where there is near-term demand or price uncertainty, allows us to again demonstrate the value proposition of two-step distribution. I'm now on slide nine. As we look forward to Q2, EWP volumes will be dependent upon new home sales and the pace at which builders begin new starts. Our EWP order files improved seasonally as we entered Q2, and we expect EWP volumes to increase by mid- to high-single digits sequentially. On EWP pricing, we expect to experience low-single-digit sequential declines as competition for share persists. In plywood, we expect seasonal strengthening and a partial restart at Oakdale to result in mid-single-digit sequential volume increases.
On plywood pricing, quarter to date realizations are consistent with our Q1 average. The partial operating status at Oakdale is expected to negatively impact our financial results by roughly $5 million in Q2, independent of market conditions. With regard to BMD sales, April's daily sales pace accelerated from the strengthening we saw in March and was approximately 13% higher than the Q1 of 2025 sales pace of $22.3 million per day. Our daily sales pace for the balance of the quarter will be dependent upon end market demand and product pricing. Lastly, we expect approximately $38 million in total company depreciation and amortization, a 26% effective tax rate, and we have 37.6 million common shares outstanding as of 30 April. I'm now on slide ten.
We had capital expenditures of $53 million in Q1, with $31 million of spending in Wood Products and $22 million of spending in BMD. Our capital spending range for 2025 remains between $220 and $240 million. This range includes additional spending on our multi-year investments in support of our EWP production capabilities in the Southeast that we have spoken to previously. At Oakdale, impacted machine centers are restarting in phases, and we're excited to have that facility fully operational again by the end of Q2. The Thorsby I-joist line is expected to be operational in the first half of 2026. In BMD, we have made great progress on our greenfield distribution in Hondo, Texas, where construction is roughly 80% complete, and we look forward to its initial startup by the end of Q3.
Speaking to shareholder returns, we paid $10 million in regular dividends during the quarter. Our board of directors also recently approved a $0.21 per share quarterly dividend on our common stock. Shareholders of record as of 2 June will receive payment of this dividend on 18 June. Through the first four months of 2025, we repurchased $71 million of our common stock, $54 million in Q1 and another $17 million in April. Today, we have about 1.1 million shares available for repurchase under our current share repurchase program. Not unexpectedly, our cash position declined in Q1 due to seasonal increases in working capital and the previously referenced capital investments and shareholder returns.
Our balance sheet remains strong, and we continue to be dedicated to a balanced deployment of capital by investing in our existing asset base, pursuing organic growth opportunities, and returning capital to our shareholders. We also maintain the flexibility to execute M&A if opportunities emerge that align with our growth strategy. I will now turn it back over to Nate to share our business outlook and closing remarks.
Nathan Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Thanks, Kelly. I'm on slide 11. Given the current environment, 2025 end market demand expectations remain difficult to predict, with most forecasts for housing ranging between flat to mid single digit declines. Our Q1 results impacted meaningfully by seasonal factors and our purposeful strategic investments are in no way a good indicator of how end market demand and our financial results will play out for the balance of 2025. Expectations for the remainder of the year are unclear as significant macroeconomic uncertainties and elevated mortgage rates have dampened consumer and home builder confidence. However, where we do have great clarity is in the strength of our team and our ability to execute at a high level across all market conditions. We remain both steady and agile.
We'll be prepared to respond as the economic situation changes and remain resolute in our service to our customer and supplier partners. The long-term demand drivers for our business remain strong, characterized by undersupply in housing units, aging US housing stock, and elevated levels of homeowner equity. The structural demand built into the housing market and our robust balance sheet provide us the ability to stay focused on the execution of our strategy and creation of long-term value for our stakeholders. Thank you for joining us today and for your continued support and interest in Boise Cascade. We welcome any questions at this time. Rivka, would you please open the phone lines?
Operator
Thank you. At this time, we'll conduct a question-and-answer session. To ask a question, you will need to press star one one on your telephone and wait for your name to be announced. To withdraw your question, please press star one one again. Please stand by while we compile the Q&A roster. Our first question comes from the line of Susan Maklari of Goldman Sachs. Your line is now open.
Susan Maklari
Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Thank you. Good morning, everyone.
Nathan Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Morning.
Susan Maklari
Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Good morning. I wanted to start on the general line side of the business. I guess, you know, given the shifts in the macro that we've seen through the quarter, any thoughts on what you're hearing from some of your key suppliers there, positions of those inventories? You know, you also mentioned the benefit of a two-step distribution model in this environment. I guess, you know, what are you also hearing from customers and how are they leveraging that service there to help with their own inventories in the channel?
Nathan Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Hey, Susan, it's Nate. I'll start the conversation, and then Joe and Jeff and others can jump in as needed. I think overall, you know, what we're seeing is that, you know, customers specific to the general line category are really dependent on two-step distribution in terms of the out-of-warehouse support on units, job packs, pieces, maybe as compared to, you know, full heavy line direct shipments. That out-of-warehouse support continues to remain a theme, and we're seeing that in terms of both expectations from our suppliers in general line, as well as how our customers, in terms of how they're thinking about, to your point, on their working capital positions. I think the other thing that we're experiencing with our general line, which is really good, is their introduction of new products, new SKUs.
That kind of creates a different maybe narrative in the marketplace, where customers may be hesitant to bring some of those newer items in because they just don't know maybe the strength or the kind of the cadence of some of those new products. Their dependency on two-step distribution BMD remains very high. I think overall, you know, we're looked to as you know, probably even more important today just in providing those just-in-time services as our customers are managing their working capital. Again, they're working that kind of risk and reward on having inventory levels both on demand and also on price realization. Overall, it feels steady and consistent. Again, two-step distribution is really an important part of that equation.
Susan Maklari
Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Okay. Sorry, that's very helpful, Nate. You know, you mentioned that the Oakdale project is progressing. It sounds like that's gone well. You know, any thoughts as you start to bring that back online relative to the macro environment that we're in and how you're positioned in terms of ramping that up?
Troy Little
Head of Wood Products Operations, Boise Cascade
Yeah, good morning, Susan. This is Troy. Yeah, I mean, when that comes back online, the majority of that veneer goes into our EWP side. We've been buying veneer on the open market right now to supplement that. When they come back online, that veneer will shift back into the EWP. There'll be some, let's say, limited plywood volume that'll come along with that. We'll just offset what we're buying on the open market and continue and then adjust, you know, production as necessary depending on demand.
Susan Maklari
Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Okay. All right. That's helpful. Then I'm gonna squeeze one last one in, which is, you know, it was nice to see the comments on the capital allocation and, you know, the potential for the buybacks. Can you talk a bit more, how you're thinking about, those priorities for this year, just given the world that we're in and anything of note on the M&A pipeline?
Kelly Hibbs
CFO, Boise Cascade
Yeah. Hi, Sue, this is Kelly. I'll take your question in reverse order a bit here. Nothing of note on the M&A pipeline. I think, you know, there's still some inbounds, but I think, you know, given kind of this near-term uncertainty, I think it's been a little bit quieter in terms of inbounds of late. We're still certainly interested to grow via M&A if that right opportunity presents itself. In terms of capital allocation in general, our script and our narrative is very much the same. We're excited about the good amount of organic project work we have ahead of us, and we'll, you know, expect to continue to be opportunistically in a thoughtful way in the market regarding share repurchases.
Susan Maklari
Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
All right. Well, thank you all for the color, and good luck with everything.
Kelly Hibbs
CFO, Boise Cascade
Thank you, Susan.
Nathan Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Thanks, Sue.
Operator
One moment for our next question. Our next question comes from the line of Kurt Yinger of D.A. Davidson. Your line is now open.
Kurt Yinger
Research Analyst, D.A. Davidson
Great. Thanks, and good morning, everyone.
Kelly Hibbs
CFO, Boise Cascade
Morning, Kurt.
Nathan Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Morning, Kurt.
Kurt Yinger
Research Analyst, D.A. Davidson
Just wanted to start off on EWP pricing. Kelly, not to pin you down all that much, but I guess directionally, would you expect kind of Q2 versus Q1 sequential pressures to be kind of about the same or maybe even lessening a little bit? Then hoping you could also just talk a little bit more about the competitive dynamics. As you've kind of moved into March and April and seen some seasonal strengthening weather, any of those pressures may be alleviating a little bit or if there's kind of a light at the end of the tunnel that you guys are seeing at this stage.
Kelly Hibbs
CFO, Boise Cascade
Yeah, sure, Kurt. I'll start, and then maybe Nate, Troy, and others can fill in. In terms of the sequential guide, yeah, we did say low single digit again. I think we were off at roughly 3% sequentially here in Q1. You know, we still have May and June to come, and it's still a very competitive environment out there. Yeah, I guess I would guide to a similar percentage to what we experienced in Q1 in terms of sequential. Again, we'll see how May and June turn out.
In terms of the kind of underlying activity, you know, like I alluded to in my comments, the order file on EWP has seasonally strengthened, you know, pretty nicely here in April. At the end of the day, you know, we're still, you know, around a seasonally adjusted annual rate on single-family housing starts that's probably less than 1 million, right? We're still in an environment where there's still competition for share. Until we see more strength in the underlying demand, I think we'll need to see that before we see some levelization on pricing.
Nathan Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Hey, Kurt, it's Nate. Maybe just to add to that. I think, you know, generally, you know, Q2 and the kind of seasonal change represents where maybe there's overall less focus on pricing on the range of products and services, and people really get centered on execution and serving the marketplace. We'll see how that narrative plays out through the quarter. Generally, history would tell us Q2 generally is again more execution-focused and less on, you know, kind of setting up programs and some of the details around that. I think the other narrative for us is on when it comes to, you know, home builder focus, they continue to stay focused on obviously their input costs, but also cycle times.
As you think about EWP and its ability to compete, and win relative to other options that are out there, whether it's dimensional lumber or even plate and floor trusses, EWP is certainly an answer in terms of affordability and relative to open-web trusses, and also creates that kind of speed and simplicity on the job site, which again remains important for the builder. Those would be maybe two backdrops as we transition into the building season, and we'll obviously be watching both of those carefully.
Kurt Yinger
Research Analyst, D.A. Davidson
Got it. Okay. That's helpful. Thank you. Kelly, just on the Oakdale impact, the $5 million, I assume that's on a year-over-year basis. I guess with Troy's comments earlier around kind of buying open market veneer to supply EWP, is that kind of cost differential contemplated in some of the numbers you've talked about related to this outage, or would that be separate?
Kelly Hibbs
CFO, Boise Cascade
Yeah, good question, Kurt. The first part, the $5 million is sequential. Its expected impact is sequential in terms of the impact of Oakdale. We expect to continue to see some challenges there as we start up. Then in terms of the veneer spoke to, I think $8 million and $7 million impacts on EBITDA from Oakdale. In Q4 and Q1, we were buying some amount of veneer, so there's not a lot of incremental cost of veneer impact into Q2. That was more of a year-over-year impact.
Kurt Yinger
Research Analyst, D.A. Davidson
Okay. Got it. Perfect. Lastly, just on BMD, you know, it sounds like general line is pretty stable. In terms of gross margin percentage, I guess how much pressure are you seeing there in EWP? I guess we look at kind of the last two years outside of quarter-over-quarter noise, you know, you guys have been kind of 15%+ on gross margin. Is that still attainable for 2025? Given some of these dynamics, is that maybe a little bit optimistic?
Kelly Hibbs
CFO, Boise Cascade
Yeah, no, I think 15% is still certainly attainable, and we're a little bit below that this quarter. You know, didn't have a lot of opportunity on the commodity side. You know, there was some competitive pressures. I think definitely 15% is attainable given the mix shift we've seen, and especially as we head here into Q2 and Q3, where you start to see a bit of a richer product mix typically. Short answer is yes on the 15%, Kurt.
Kurt Yinger
Research Analyst, D.A. Davidson
Perfect. All right. Thank you very much.
Kelly Hibbs
CFO, Boise Cascade
Thank you.
Nathan Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Thanks, Kurt.
Operator
One moment for our next question. Our next question comes from the line of George Staphos of Bank of America Securities. Your line is now open.
George Staphos
Managing Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Bank of America Securities
Hi, everyone. Good morning. Thanks for the details. Just a couple of quick ones to tag on to the existing question that were asked. Can you talk a little bit about the competitive pressures in EWP? Are you seeing it more from existing, you know, engineered players, or are you seeing it more because of or from, you know, either dimensional or from folks producing open-web trusses? Secondly, it sounds like everything is fine here, but in terms of the 13% improvement you're seeing in daily sales so far in Q2, any change or trend that we should be aware of in terms of mix velocity? You know, again, sounded like everything's fine here, but just wanna check that box, guys.
Nathan Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Maybe on the EWP, let me see. George, it's Nate. Just on the EWP side of things, I think, you know, what we're seeing is, you know, the narrative on two-by-tens and open-web trusses is largely consistent and steady. Not a lot there. Where we generally see the competitive challenges is with EWP producers. That's something that, you know, we are committed to making sure we're competitive and in market each and every day for our customers, both our, you know, direct customers as well as through the channel. That's been the backdrop in terms of the competitive nature, and that's been in place here for several quarters.
That would be, you know, probably, you know, kind of our current view on EWP and what we're seeing and what we're expecting there relative to competitive nature.
Kelly Hibbs
CFO, Boise Cascade
Yeah. I guess the second part of your question, George, was around the 13% sequential increase we've seen so far in the daily sales pace in BMD, which that math tells you it's about $25 million a day through April compared to the $22.3 we experienced in Q1. You know, I wouldn't say there's any big mix shift or anything like that. It's really just a function of, you know, the spring building season, better weather, and you know, the really out of the gates here, pretty strong in April, which is great.
If you do the math, $25 million-ish a day times 64 days, you know, you'll see, you know, BMD kick out $1.6 billion or so in revenue in Q2, which would be up $200 million sequentially. That gives you a good sense of the gross margin dollar opportunity and the better leverage you can get on our cost base that, you know, we expect to put up certainly an improved number here in Q2 of BMD.
George Staphos
Managing Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Bank of America Securities
Yeah. Kelly, I appreciate that. What I was getting at, and maybe could have posed the question differently, just it seems like the momentum has actually continued or accelerated. It's not like we're at 13%, but there's been a fade more recently. I was more or less just confirming that or not, if you wanna comment. Along with that, can you give us a quick comment on the door strategy, how that's working? And are there any elements of the supply chain into BMD that we, you know, should be mindful of relative to tariffs? You know, any difficulties getting product that you need, or you're in pretty good shape there? Thanks and good luck in the quarter.
Kelly Hibbs
CFO, Boise Cascade
Yeah. Yeah, just a quick follow-up. Yeah. That pace I referenced has, you know, has continued, you know, through the first few days in April, and so we feel good about that. Then in terms of the doors and supply chain, I'll let Jeff lead the conversation there.
Jeff Strom
COO, Boise Cascade
Yeah. Hey, this is Jeff. On the door side, that strategy is going well. I'll tell you, the acquisitions we made, the newer shops, they're growing and you can see it. You know, when you greenfield one as we have, you know, it's a process, and it takes time, and they certainly are. Then you have the acquisitions, and they're obviously faster. You can see them growing. Then the legacy ones we have, they've picked up significantly. You know, it's working just the way we want it.
George Staphos
Managing Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Bank of America Securities
Okay. On tariffs and supply chain?
Nathan Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
George.
Yes. It's George. It's Nate. Yeah. I would say in tariffs overall, for both wood products and BMD, there's kind of limited impact. You know, for us, it's a you know, pretty defined risk both in wood products. Most of our production, as you know, is US-based, and so that doesn't really represent an issue you know, for us in wood products, given the current environment today. For distribution, as you know, our philosophy overall is to you know, when we have to pass along you know, pricing you know, changes or cost increases that we experience. Tariffs would represent you know, a very similar theme as to anything else that we would think about there.
Specific to, there are some certain products, as you think about in our general line, many of our metal products are imported. In some cases, George, there's limited options on where, you know, where you can pull those materials from. I guess the good news here is we, you know, have some familiarity with this story, just given the COVID issues in terms of, you know, the resiliency and kind of the redundancy in some cases with our supply chain, and that remains, you know, part of our plan going forward. Relatively, the, you know, the impact is very modest today, and if anything, would be general line just on some of those, like, again, kind of the metal products would be the area that we're currently focused.
George Staphos
Managing Director and Senior Equity Analyst, Bank of America Securities
Thanks so much, Nate. Good luck in the quarter, guys.
Nathan Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Thanks.
Operator
One moment for our next question. Our next question comes from the line of Jeff Stevenson of Loop Capital. Your line is now open.
Zack Pacheco
VP of Equity Research, Loop Capital Markets
Hey, good morning, guys. This is actually Zack Pacheco on for Jeff this morning.
Kelly Hibbs
CFO, Boise Cascade
Hey, Zack.
Zack Pacheco
VP of Equity Research, Loop Capital Markets
Hey, how you guys doing? Maybe to start, given the current pricing environment, can you just provide some more color specifically on how you're looking at LVL kind of through the remainder of the year, more on the volume side? I believe last quarter share gains were called out as a positive. Just curious if there's any update from a share gain perspective. Thanks.
Troy Little
Head of Wood Products Operations, Boise Cascade
Yeah. As Kelly mentioned, you know, Q1 we were down 3%, not quite as much as the housing starts. Also he referenced the fact that so far starting into Q2, we're starting to see LVL in particular actually start outpacing our production. So we're starting to see our inventories come down there. Then as indicated, you know, we're still looking for that, you know, seasonal bump in volumes that we've indicated in the charts. Unless you've got any more on that.
Kelly Hibbs
CFO, Boise Cascade
Yeah, no. I think Troy covered it pretty well other than, I guess what I would add is that, I think we've pretty consistently shown that our share of production as well as our volumes relative to single-family starts have looked very strong. Again, we think that's very much a function of, one, having best-in-class products and best-in-class distribution tied together, and we continue to believe that's the right approach.
Zack Pacheco
VP of Equity Research, Loop Capital Markets
Understood. Maybe just quickly on BMD, how attainable or how confident is the team on a sequential improvement in terms of EBITDA margins to at or above 5% in the next quarter, given the adverse weather you experienced in this quarter? Or do you think softer residential demand fundamentals will continue to weigh on segment margins? Thanks.
Kelly Hibbs
CFO, Boise Cascade
I feel good about, and I alluded to this a bit in my comments, that March, you know, when we saw a more normal sales pace, we got our EBITDA margins back to what you've seen in recent quarters, you know, kind of that mid five range, if you will. Given where we've started in April and given the pace we've seen, we feel really good about our opportunity to again be, you know, be in the mid fives for Q2. Then a couple other comments here from Jo.
Joanna Barney
Head of Building Materials Distribution Operations, Boise Cascade
Yeah. Hi there. So as far as competitive positioning in the market, you know, I think we're set up really well. Our national footprint allows us to shift our volume into pockets of strength across the country, also helps us to service the national dealers, who want and need consistent service across the country. You know, we're aligned with many of the big builders and the dealers and their strength in times of market weakness, but at the same time, our decentralized model allows us to support and serve the local and regional dealers and builders as well and be flexible to their needs. We've got great partnerships with our customers, with our suppliers, and really our integrated model with manufacturing, you know, is a key part of driving our success.
Zack Pacheco
VP of Equity Research, Loop Capital Markets
Makes sense. Thanks for the color.
Kelly Hibbs
CFO, Boise Cascade
Thank you, Zack.
Operator
As a reminder, to ask a question, please press star one one on your telephone and wait for your name to be announced. Our next question comes from the line of Ketan Mamtora of BMO Capital Markets. Your line is now open.
Ketan Mamtora
Director of Equity Research, BMO Capital Markets
Thank you and good morning. Perhaps to start with, on Q2 EWP volumes, if I'm doing my math correctly here, it sounds like on I-joist, you know, volumes will be down about double digits on a year-over-year basis. Kelly, can you talk about sort of, you know, puts and takes, you know, what's kind of driving that, you know, sort of a pretty meaningful year-over-year decline in volume?
Kelly Hibbs
CFO, Boise Cascade
Yeah. I think it's really just a function of housing starts last year versus the housing start assumption for this year, Ketan. It's really that. It's not, in my view, a loss of market share or a change in usage in terms of floor products. It's not that. It's really just a function of the underlying market conditions today.
Ketan Mamtora
Director of Equity Research, BMO Capital Markets
I see. Okay. Got it. You know, if I look at your inventories at the end of Q1 versus kind of your total inventories at the end of, you know, Q1 of last year, it's again up like, I don't know, 12, 13 percent, something in that range. Can you sort of talk to how you sort of feel about the overall level of inventories given the housing backdrop, which has been, you know, sort of choppier? You know, we've talked about things off to a slower than expected start.
Kelly Hibbs
CFO, Boise Cascade
Yeah. Let me let Jeff kind of field that initially, the question around inventory and what we're seeing, where we're at here in Q1 and relative to our expectations.
Jeff Strom
COO, Boise Cascade
Yes, Jeff. Yeah, our inventory position, you know, feel good about it. When the winter buys came and opportunities for buys, we fully took advantage of that and leaned into that pretty heavily. We also look at, you know, with the market that we're in right now, we know it is very much a distribution-friendly market, and people are relying on us. Our suppliers are relying on us to have, and our customers are relying on us to have and get them there on time. We've leaned into that and made sure that we're stocked and ready for that. On the dealer side of things, what we're seeing out there, without a doubt, it is lean overall.
Nathan Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
A couple areas where it might be heavy if they leaned in for tariffs, but overall it is lean, and people are relying on distribution, and we're ready to serve.
Ketan Mamtora
Director of Equity Research, BMO Capital Markets
Understood. That's helpful color. You know, maybe last one for Nate. You know, there's been a couple of transactions here recently, you know, one you know on kind of you know one of your kind of supplier side and then one on the you know pro dealer side, some pretty meaningful transactions. How do you you know sort of think about potential impact, if any, you know, over the next several years here?
Nathan Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Yeah, good question, Ketan. I think when it comes to your point, some of the consolidation that's taken place, both upstream and downstream, you know, from Boise Cascade, you know, that has been, you know, a theme here over the past number of years and certainly is continuing, and obviously in some important examples in front of us today. I think as we you know we are, I think, well-positioned in the marketplace and well-positioned with those relationships. I think the counsel that we continue to work internally and externally is we're gonna stay really focused on the here and now and execute at a very high level, for the benefit of both those suppliers and what our customers deserve and expect, going forward.
I think we are in a very important part of the equation for, you know, our suppliers and we've got to continue to earn that each and every day. Same with our customers. The consolidation, those trends, those have been taking place. We expect those likely to take place going forward. That it really requires us to make sure that we're focused on executing at a very, very high level each and every day.
Ketan Mamtora
Director of Equity Research, BMO Capital Markets
Got it. That's very helpful. Good luck.
Nathan Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Thank you.
Operator
One moment for our next question. Our next question comes from the line of Reuben Garner of Benchmark. Your line is now open.
Reuben Garner
Senior Analyst, Benchmark
Thank you. Good morning, guys. Apologies if I repeat anything. I missed the first part of the call. Big picture question for you, and correct me if I'm looking at this wrong, but I think the volume for I-joist and LVL is kind of round-tripped back to pre-2020 levels for you guys. But on a higher level of starts, is the difference between what you would've seen back then and today, size and type of homes or is there some other dynamic? Are you guys thinking about, you know, your volume versus your price differently than maybe you did five or six years ago? Just any color there would be helpful.
Nathan Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Yeah. Reuben, it's Nate. You know, that's a good question. I think in terms of, you know, what we're experiencing, I don't think it's anything in terms of, you know, kind of change at I-joist versus maybe open web or dimensional lumber. You know, there can be some around the edges. I think much of that is probably around maybe home size and the home footprint. That's, and also where that start resides. Some examples, for example, if you're in, you know, a market like Phoenix, it's a slab-on-grade market, single-story construction. That represents a much different opportunity than compared to, you know, a Denver, Colorado, as an example, where typically two-story construction with a basement.
I think, you know, in terms of where that start resides and the strength that we've seen in, you know, the Sunshine States, you know, the Florida, Texas, and Arizona, yeah, I think that's been a contributing factor in terms of what that real floor opportunity represents for, you know, for I-joist and framing materials here today in 2025.
Reuben Garner
Senior Analyst, Benchmark
Nate, as that relates to price, I mean, your pricing is still up nicely since then. I know I'm sure you have a ton of areas of inflation in your own regard, but how do we think about just kind of downside from here given where the volume environment is? What does the supply or capacity utilization for the industry look like today versus maybe what it did in that period five, six years ago?
Kelly Hibbs
CFO, Boise Cascade
Yeah. Capacity realization today for Q1 for us, we ran at a pretty strong rate given the environment. We were kind of between 75% and 80%. In April, we were above that level. It was probably low 80s. I don't have 2019 still in my memory bank. I think our operating rate relative to the demand environment today, we feel good about. Again, having the connection between manufacturing and distribution is important.
Reuben Garner
Senior Analyst, Benchmark
Great. Thanks, guys. Good luck in this coming quarter.
Nathan Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Thank you, Reuben.
Kelly Hibbs
CFO, Boise Cascade
Thanks, Reuben.
Operator
I am showing no further questions at this time. I would now like to turn it back to Nate Jorgensen, the CEO, for closing remarks.
Nathan Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Great. Thanks. We appreciate everyone joining us this morning for our update and earnings call. Thank you for your continued interest and support of Boise Cascade. Be safe and be well. Thank you.
Operator
Thank you for your participation in today's conference. This concludes the program. You may now disconnect.

content.text:
Operator
Good morning. My name is Josh, and I will be your conference facilitator today. At this time, I would like to welcome everyone to Boise Cascade's Q4 and full year 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All lines have been placed on mute to prevent any background noise. After the speaker's remarks, there will be a question-and-answer period. It is now my pleasure to introduce you to Chris Forrey, Vice President, Finance and Investor Relations, Boise Cascade. Mr. Forrey, you may begin your conference.
Chris Forrey
VP of Finance and Investor Relations, Boise Cascade
Thank you, Josh, and good morning, everyone. I'd like to welcome you to Boise Cascade's Q4 2024 earnings call and business update. Joining me on today's call are Nate Jorgensen, our CEO; Kelly Hibbs, our CFO and Treasurer; Troy Little, Head of our Wood Products Operations; and Jeff Strom, our recently announced COO and former head of our Building Materials Distribution Operations. Turning to slide two. This call will contain forward-looking statements. Please review the warning statements in our press release, on the presentation slides, and in our filings with the SEC regarding the risks associated with these forward-looking statements. Also, please note that the appendix includes reconciliations from our GAAP net income to EBITDA and adjusted EBITDA, and segment income to segment EBITDA. I will now turn the call over to Nate.
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Thanks, Chris. Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us for our earnings call today. On slide three, I'll start by highlighting some of our accomplishments as I reflect on our 2024 results. We reported full year net income of $376.4 million or $9.57 per diluted share. We grew our distribution business through our organic and acquisition initiatives, made progress on significant capital investments to support our EWP growth strategy, and provided meaningful capital returns to our shareholders. I'm grateful to our associates as they've shown commitment to our values and steadfast support for our customers, suppliers, and each other. Let me now turn to the Q4 results.
Total US housing starts and single-family housing starts decreased 6% and 4% respectively compared to the prior-year quarter. Our consolidated Q4 sales of $1.6 billion were down 5% from Q4 2023. Our net income was $68.9 million or $0.78 per share compared to net income of $97.5 million or $2.44 per share in the year-ago quarter. Our year-ago quarter earnings per share were negatively impacted by approximately $0.18 per share from accelerated depreciation related to the Chapman, Alabama lumber facility closure and transaction expenses for the BROSCO acquisition. Kelly will now walk through our segment financial results, give some early insights on Q1, and then provide an update on our capital allocation in more detail, after which I'll provide our outlook before we take your questions. Kelly?
Kelly Hibbs
CFO and Treasurer, Boise Cascade
Thank you, Nate. Wood Products sales in Q4, including sales for our distribution segment, were $419.7 million, down 7% compared to Q4 2023. Wood Products segment EBITDA was $56.6 million compared to EBITDA of $92.7 million reported in the year-ago quarter. The decrease in segment EBITDA was due primarily to lower EWP and plywood sales prices. In BMD, our sales in the quarter were $1.4 billion, down 4% from Q4 2023. BMD reported segment EBITDA of $84.5 million in Q4 compared to segment EBITDA of $80.6 million in the prior-year quarter. Despite the sales decline, a 60 basis points increase in gross margin percentage positioned BMD to deliver comparable year-over-year gross margin dollars.
In addition, BMD's general administrative expenses decreased by $3.6 million, due primarily to acquisition-related expenses in the prior year quarter for the acquisition of BROSCO. Turning to slide five. On a year-over-year basis, Q4 volumes for LVL increased an impressive 11%, and I-joist volumes were down 2%, both better than the 4% year-over-year decline in single-family starts, which we believe is a testament to the strength of our tightly aligned manufacturing and nationwide distribution capabilities. As expected, seasonal declines in construction activity drove lower volumes on a sequential basis, with LVL and I-joist volumes down 8% and 10% respectively.
Again, for this comparative period, our volume changes were better than underlying activity in single-family starts would imply. At current demand levels, competition for share is prevalent in the marketplace today, and our sequential LVL pricing for LVL and I-joist were down 2% and 1% respectively. Turning to Slide 6. Our Q4 plywood sales volume was 371 million feet compared to 363 million feet in Q4 2023. The $350 per thousand average plywood net sales price in the Q4 was down 7% on a year-over-year basis. However, plywood net sales prices were up 5% sequentially. We experienced higher plywood pricing through the H1 of the Q4 before expected seasonal decline set in, with December average price realizations of approximately $340 per thousand. Moving to slide seven and eight.
BMD's year-over-year Q4 sales decline of 4% was driven by a 2% decrease in both sales price and volume. By product line, commodity sales decreased 4%, general line product sales increased 1%, and sales of EWP decreased 11%. As I alluded to earlier, BMD's Q4 gross margin percentage was 15.8%, up 60 basis points year-over-year. In particular, our commodity inventory position, coupled with strengthening commodity markets during the H1 of the Q4, provided tailwinds for our commodity margins. BMD's EBITDA margin was 5.9% for the quarter, up from the 5.4% reported in the year ago and up 30 basis points sequentially. Very strong results in a seasonally slower quarter. I'm now on slide nine.
Weather has made for a difficult start to the quarter as we have had a couple days of unplanned downtime across several of our manufacturing and distribution locations. As we look forward to our expectations for Q1, EWP volumes are expected to increase modestly from Q4 levels, and EWP pricing is expected to reflect low single-digit sequential declines. In plywood, the significant modernization projects at our Oakdale facility are progressing well. As planned, that facility will be down for the entirety of Q1 and is expected to operate near 50% of capacity in Q2. As a result, our plywood volumes and cost absorption will be negatively impacted in the near term.
For Q1, we expect plywood volumes to decline mid to high single digits sequentially and that we will incur negative cost impacts of approximately $17 million due to the Oakdale downtime. On plywood pricing, quarter to date realizations are approximately 3% below Q4 averages. With regards to BMD sales, seasonal impacts are evident with our quarter to date daily sales pace about 8% below our Q4 daily sales averages. We'd expect activity to strengthen as we move towards the spring building season. Now on slide 10. We had capital expenditures of $230 million in 2024, with $122 million of spending in Wood Products and $108 million of spending in BMD. Looking forward to 2025, we expect our capital spending to be between $220 million and $240 million.
This range includes additional spending on our multi-year investments in support of EWP production capabilities, including adding I-joist production at our Thorsby, Alabama EWP facility and the significant modernization projects at our Oakdale, Louisiana veneer and plywood mill. In BMD, we are making great progress on our greenfield distribution center in Hondo, Texas. Activity at the Walterboro, South Carolina, greenfield has been slow, but we expect to gain momentum there in the back half of 2025. Speaking to shareholder returns in 2024, we paid $229 million in regular and special dividends, which was comprised of $0.82 per share in regular quarterly dividends, and a $5 per share special dividend. Our board of directors also recently approved a $0.21 per share quarterly dividend on our common stock. Shareholders of record as of 24 February 2024 will receive payment of this dividend on 19 March 2024.
For the 13 months ended January 2025, we have repurchased approximately 1.75 million shares or 4.5% of our outstanding shares for approximately $225 million. Today, we have about 1.6 million shares available for repurchase under our share repurchase program. As our actions demonstrate, we continue to strive for a balanced approach to capital allocation that includes ongoing investments in our existing asset base, organic growth projects, and returns to our shareholders. Our balance sheet also gives us the flexibility to pursue M&A if opportunities surface that align with our strategy. I will now turn it back over to Nate to share our business outlook and closing remarks.
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Thanks, Kelly. I'm on slide 11. Current industry forecasts for total US housing starts are around 1.35 million for 2025, essentially flat with actual housing starts in 2024, as reported by the US Census Bureau. Single-family housing starts in 2024 outpaced 2023 levels by 7% and are expected to again be around 1 million, the 1 million level, despite the affordability challenges consumers are facing in the current rate environment. Multifamily starts declined sharply in 2024 and are expected to continue to face headwinds in 2025 due to prohibitive capital costs for developers, combined with elevated levels of multifamily unit completions in both 2023 and 2024.
For home improvement spending, we expect 2025 to reflect modest growth as the age of US housing stock, elevated levels of homeowner equity, and some recent improvement in existing home sales will provide a favorable backdrop for repair and remodel spending. While uncertainties around the macroeconomy and policy decisions from the new administration make it challenging to predict the near-term demand environment, our constructive view on the medium and longer-term housing fundamentals remains. Which affords us the ability to maintain a clear focus on our strategy and the execution of our growth initiatives. Lastly, I would like to take the opportunity to congratulate Jeff Strom and Jo Barney on their recently announced promotions. Both are seasoned and accomplished leaders, and look forward to their continued contributions in their new roles.
These changes were part of our intentional or strategic succession planning process as we position the company for continued service and support to our shareholders, our stakeholders in the future. Thank you for joining us on our call today and your continuing interest in support of Boise Cascade. We welcome any questions at this time. Josh, would you please open the phone lines?
Operator
Thank you. As a reminder, to ask a question, please press star one one on your telephone and wait for your name to be announced. To withdraw your question, please press star one one again. One moment for questions. Our first question comes from Kurt Yinger with D.A. Davidson. You may proceed.
Kurt Yinger
SVP and Research Analyst, D.A. Davidson
Great. Thanks, and good morning, everyone.
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Good morning, Kurt.
Kurt Yinger
SVP and Research Analyst, D.A. Davidson
I just wanted to start off on tariffs, and we have pretty robust data on lumber and OSB and how important Canadian supply is there, but EWP is kind of a murkier picture. I guess first off, could you maybe frame, Canadian supply relative to US consumption. Maybe where you run into some of those call it secondary suppliers in the market, and how you're thinking about opportunities that could arise for Boise if we were to see some tariff implementation?
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Hey, Kurt, it's Nate. Let me start that, and Kelly and others can jump in. Yeah, I think in terms of the tariff question, obviously there's more unknowns than knowns relative to that. To your point, there's clarity in terms of how much volume is moving across, I think, largely from an industry perspective and for Boise Cascade from Canada into the US, and some of that is obviously around some of our commodities.
If you think about the, some of the other items that we bring across the border, whether it's web stock or other items, it's, I think, in terms of the impact. We've done a lot of modeling and a lot of work, Kurt, just to make sure we understand, some of the actions and decisions we may need to take as a result of tariffs. There's nothing that, we've concluded at this stage in terms of, anything immediate that we'll be doing in the marketplace.
At this point, the other, thing that we're, looking at is the demand environment, in terms of the ripple effect on affordability as we've talked about, is a potential challenge with tariffs. As we think about, the consequences of what could take place, again, not just on, the lumber items, but other items as well, that's gonna be, something that we're watching carefully and closely, but we've done a lot of work just to make sure we're prepared to move forward should, that tariff arrive. Again, there's a lot of discussion debate on when and if that's possible.
Maybe with that, Kelly, anything you would add just in terms of, how we're thinking about that and just, maybe a backdrop on that?
Kelly Hibbs
CFO and Treasurer, Boise Cascade
Yeah, sure, Nate. Yeah, good to hear you, Kurt. Yeah, for us, you think about it in our two segments. As you well know, our manufacturing is substantially based in the US. To Nate's point, we would have some cost pressure from OSB web stock that we do get from Canada. We are very well-positioned there and so feel good about our ability to operate, again, given that, to Nate's point, there's a lot more unknowns than there are knowns in that space.
In BMD, if there are tariffs, and we do import a lot of commodity products from Canada, for example, if there were higher costs there, our intent would be to push those through and maintain our normal margin percentage. That's kinda how we play the market every day, if you will. That would be our expectation. The broader concern is probably if the tariffs end up, to Nate's point, causing further affordability challenges, do we have demand destruction? That would be a bigger, broader concern.
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Maybe just to close out on that, Kurt, I think when you think about the some of the policy uncertainty that's out there, and even the weather that Kelly described, it's just the risk reward. There's a lot of hesitancy in the marketplace. I think you know we're seeing and experiencing that. I think for us the good news is that we're seeing continued strength out of warehouse as people mitigate and manage that risk reward. Our warehouse business remains steady. You can you know certainly hear the influence of that policy risk in the conversations across the industry.
Kurt Yinger
SVP and Research Analyst, D.A. Davidson
Right. Okay. No, that's great color. I appreciate it. Moving on to EWP pricing, it's been this slide over the last two years and, maybe some of that's wringing out some excess margin, and now it seems like more supply and demand finding a balance. You talked about some of the competitive dynamics in terms of securing share. As we look out to 2025, thinking about maybe a flattish housing starts environment, do you feel like the market is pretty close to finding that equilibrium, or are there any other big variables on the supply side that you're watching more closely?
Kelly Hibbs
CFO and Treasurer, Boise Cascade
Yeah, Kurt, this is Kelly again. I don't think on the supply side, I don't know that there's a lot of variables there. I mean, there's no new capacity coming online here in the near term. But I do think if we're in a 1.35 total or a 1.0 single-family environment, I think there will continue to be competition for share. And so we've continued to see that in some modest price erosion. And if the environment stays like that, we'd expect to see some erosion. And then there could be some seasonally stronger periods where maybe it's a little less competitive at times.
There's no reason for us to believe we won't continue to see some level of erosion if demand stays where it is.
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Hey, Kurt, Nate. Maybe the other thing I would just add is when you think about EWP relative to other options, I think it still represents the right answer for the builder in terms of, the cycle time at the job site, the simplicity and, relative to other options and materials that might be available. As we think of the backdrop of EWP overall, I think it's again favorable in terms of what the builder is looking and needing to get done and at the job site. We feel good about, that being a continuing to be a tailwind for EWP moving forward.
Kurt Yinger
SVP and Research Analyst, D.A. Davidson
Got it. If I could just sneak one more in following up on that. I mean, historically, I don't think you guys have ever viewed pricing on lumber as a huge driver of substitution between solid sawn and I-joist or open web floor trusses. If we were to see more upward pressure there on the commodity pricing, is that something on the margin that you think could be a potential positive, or is there not really any historical evidence to support that?
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Yeah, generally, Kurt, it's most of the builders generally stay, pretty true to, to the product that whether it's dimensional lumber, to your point, open web floor trusses or EWP. I think there's a fair bit of consistency there. To your point, if they're at the margin, that probably, if there's higher pressure on pricing on dimensional lumber, as an example, that'll probably create some, discussion and some opportunities for a potential conversion. I think the builder, they'll continue to look at the affordability side of things. That's, certainly first and foremost on their mind.
Part of that affordability is not just materials, but also, speed on the job site and simplicity at the job site as well.
Kurt Yinger
SVP and Research Analyst, D.A. Davidson
Right. Okay, awesome. Appreciate all the color, guys. Thank you.
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Thanks, Kurt.
Operator
Thank you. As a reminder, to ask a question, please press star one one on your telephone. Our next question comes from Susan Maklari with Goldman Sachs. You may proceed.
Susan Maklari
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Thank you. Good morning, everyone.
Kelly Hibbs
CFO and Treasurer, Boise Cascade
Hey, Sue.
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Morning, Sue.
Susan Maklari
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Good morning, and congrats to Jeff. Good to have you on the call.
Jeff Strom
COO, Boise Cascade
Thank you, Sue. I appreciate that.
Susan Maklari
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Yeah. I wanna start by talking a bit about the operating environment. You mentioned the impact to weather that'll come through in Q1, but can you also talk a bit about how we should think of the weather, the macro environment, and what you're hearing as the builders are starting to get into the early parts of the selling season?
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Yeah. Thanks, Sue. It's Nate. I think, the builders, there's the affordability remains, probably first and foremost in the conversation. I think when you look at, home prices, when you look at cost of money, that remains front and center. They've been, some of the builders, as have been active in terms of buying down rates. I think that's been an important part of what we experienced as we closed 2024, and I think what, the builders are describing in terms of 2025.
I think in terms of the medium to longer term, I think there's still a lot of, optimism and, belief that we still are underbuilt as a country. I think that narrative remains if more, again, probably from the medium to longer term. In the short term, again, I think there's some complexity and unknowns, and part of that is certainly around, the economy and what could be happening there, including things like tariffs that could drive that. But this, that maybe hesitancy is maybe more of the theme that we've heard here, over the past couple of weeks. I don't think that's, for me, there's a lot of anxiety.
It's simply people are probably a little bit more measured, at least in the short term, until they have a better view of what the environment is. I think the home builders remain still, optimistic about, certainly the future. I think in the near term, they're gonna manage it on a, day by day basis to make sure that they're making the right choices and decisions, for each of their stakeholders, including their shareholders.
Susan Maklari
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Yeah. Okay. That's helpful color. Thinking about the environment and the fact that maybe there's some increasing competition on commodity EWP products, can you talk about the potential benefits and the more resilient nature of the general line part of the business and how that could perhaps be a relative offset in this kind of situation?
Jeff Strom
COO, Boise Cascade
Hey, Sue, this is Jeff. The general line, it continues to hold up very well. That being said, it is competitive out there. As things slow down and people are looking for market share, it does get incredibly competitive. We're having to keep our eye on that and react where we need to.
Susan Maklari
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Okay. That's helpful. I just want to sneak one more in, which is, it was nice to see the buybacks that came through in 2024. As you do think about your approach to capital allocation for this year, can you talk a bit about shareholder returns and how you're thinking about buybacks versus perhaps the special dividend? Just any color there.
Kelly Hibbs
CFO and Treasurer, Boise Cascade
Yeah, sure, Sue. Sue, let me, start maybe a little more broadly, and then we can work our way to your specific question. Capital allocation, obviously, as you've seen in the materials, we have a, the second year of a, for us, a pretty heavy capital spending program. That is going to be the main focus here is to make sure we execute on our capital spending objectives, go get M&A if we find something that makes sense. Specific to shareholder returns, I expect us to opportunistically stay in the market in buying shares on a more consistent basis.
Like you've seen recently, and then special dividend, that will be a conversation with the board, but I'd anticipate that'd be more later in the year, more like a Q3 event if the board chooses to do that. Again, that could be also dependent upon, what might we find in the M&A space and, or do we seek out and find some additional organic growth opportunities.
Susan Maklari
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Okay. Well, I got an answer from all three of you, which I appreciate. Good luck to everyone. We'll talk soon.
Kelly Hibbs
CFO and Treasurer, Boise Cascade
Thank you.
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Thank you.
Operator
Thank you. Our next question comes from Mike Roxland with Truist Securities. You may proceed.
Mike Roxland
Managing Director and Equity Research, Truist Securities
Yeah. Thanks very much for taking my questions, and congrats on all the progress.
Kelly Hibbs
CFO and Treasurer, Boise Cascade
Morning. Morning, Mike.
Mike Roxland
Managing Director and Equity Research, Truist Securities
Morning. Yeah, Kelly, as you noted, BMD margin was strong in Q4, certainly better than we expected, despite some sales pace deterioration during the quarter. Mix was also a little more unfavorable versus Q3. Can you help us understand then, how you generated a higher sequential margin, especially as margins are seasonally lower sequentially? Was any of that due to Nate's point on increasing warehouse sales? Just any color you can provide about the, around the margin and how you were able to achieve that type of margin in Q4.
Kelly Hibbs
CFO and Treasurer, Boise Cascade
Yeah. There's several components in there, and you hit on several of them, Mike. The one is, yeah, warehouse and, again, the uncertainty in the marketplace and how that increases reliance from our customers on our inventory position. That helped. Then I would also say, commodities had a decent little run the first part, the H1 of the Q4, and that really gave us so some tailwinds that we were able to to capture in the Q4.
Mike Roxland
Managing Director and Equity Research, Truist Securities
Got it. When you think about, take the transition from Q4 to Q1 in terms of EBITDA margin, how should we think about it? Because obviously you're guiding to a sales pace that has deteriorated further in Q1 relative to Q4. Obviously, you've cited winter weather, there's uncertainty. I get all that. Are you able to maintain that level in Q4 or should we see some type of erosion because of the sales pace deterioration relative to Q4?
Kelly Hibbs
CFO and Treasurer, Boise Cascade
Yeah. We will see erosion from Q4 for sure, Mike. I mean, given the 8% sales pace decline that we've seen so far in the Q1 compared to the Q4, and that coupled with, no tailwinds in terms of across any product lines in terms of price appreciation, yeah, we will not report that same level of EBITDA margin here in the Q1.
Mike Roxland
Managing Director and Equity Research, Truist Securities
Got it. One last one from me. Can you help us understand what drove the growth in LVL? Obviously, very strong growth in Q4, up 11%. I think single-family starts down 4% to 5%. Did you gain share against your peers? Is that something that you expect to continue? Just help us frame what happened and how we should think about the going forward.
Kelly Hibbs
CFO and Treasurer, Boise Cascade
Yeah. Yeah, that's a great segue for me to give a great shout out to the combined efforts of the Wood Products and BMD sales teams. Very active this year in, getting out and selling our value proposition, and that's really showing up in our volumes. Like I alluded to in my comments, volumes better than what underlying single-family starts would imply. Really good execution. Again, that linkage between our manufacturing and distribution showed up really well.
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
The other thing for me, Mike, it's Nate, is as you think about LVL, and, the applications for that in terms of beams and headers, it's really a steady and probably, growing application opportunity. We've talked at times about, competitiveness on EWP, specifically with I-joist, open web floor trusses, and dimensional lumber. The complexity of designs and such continues to, support beam and header use.
I think, in terms of the backdrop on, the opportunity and how that shows up for that product category specifically, we feel good about what that represents and obviously that's consistent with how we thought about continuing to invest and grow that part of our business from a production standpoint. Yeah, thanks for, calling that out. Again, we feel good about where we finished and really what's in front of us is somewhat independent of the housing market.
Mike Roxland
Managing Director and Equity Research, Truist Securities
Got it. Great call. Appreciate it, and wishing you the best of luck, this year.
Kelly Hibbs
CFO and Treasurer, Boise Cascade
Thanks, Mike.
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Thanks, Mike.
Operator
Our next question comes from George Staphos with Bank of America Securities. You may proceed.
George Staphos
Managing Director, Bank of America Securities
Hi, everyone. Good morning. Thanks for the details. Congrats to Jeff and Jo. My first question. Maybe I'll segue off of the discussion we were just having with Mike. Given the complexity of homes and the way that this is supporting greater demand for beam and header use, on the other hand, you talk about inflation affordability. What can you talk about whether, size of home, conservation materials, how that might be impacting, if at all, demand for EWP as you're seeing it right now? Relatedly, I know it's hard to parse this precisely, right? Are you seeing more of the price erosion coming from competition against other EWP products in the market, or is it coming from dimensional? Is it coming from trusses? How should we think about that?
Kelly Hibbs
CFO and Treasurer, Boise Cascade
Yeah. I'll start, George. To answer your second question first-
George Staphos
Managing Director, Bank of America Securities
Morning, Kelly.
Kelly Hibbs
CFO and Treasurer, Boise Cascade
Yeah, the price erosion is related to competition for light EWP products. It's not from competing products like dimensional lumber, as you referenced. It's EWP.
George Staphos
Managing Director, Bank of America Securities
Okay
Kelly Hibbs
CFO and Treasurer, Boise Cascade
You're right. In terms of how does the demand environment or how does the size of homes impact demand? Yes, it will. If you have smaller homes, that will create less footage used in a home. Not necessarily in terms of the applications or products that the builders will use, but if the footprint is smaller, the usage will be smaller.
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Hey, George. It's Nate. Yeah, maybe just to Kelly's point, I think.
George Staphos
Managing Director, Bank of America Securities
Hey, Nate. Morning. Yeah.
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Good morning. When you think about, the square footage, I think that's, to me, probably focuses more on the I-joist, statement in terms of that, kind of consumption. And certainly beams and headers are part of that and wall framing. Again, when you look at the designs today, even though those footprints are getting a little bit smaller, the complexity continues to grow in terms of the open spaces and the expectations around that. I think that backdrop and theme remains, and that's really supportive of, the beams and our LVL growth as a result. The other piece of it, as is housing starts are really the consumption of EWP is really dependent on a geographic basis.
Consumption in Florida is different than in Colorado. As you think about where that housing start resides, that has influence in terms of,-
George Staphos
Managing Director, Bank of America Securities
Right
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
what's expected as well. Overall, I think the beam and header market is generally has a little more stability around it, in part based upon, some of the construction techniques that remain out there.
George Staphos
Managing Director, Bank of America Securities
Nate, I mean, just to summarize it, and look, we're never gonna hold you to this. We just wanna understand what you're seeing in terms of market. Even with some of the headwinds, on square footage and like your view, holding everything else constant, dangerous phrase there, is that you should see incrementally better demand for EWP because of those points on complexity of design and the related factors. Would that be fair?
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Yeah. I would say more on the the beam and header side of things, George, as opposed to the-
George Staphos
Managing Director, Bank of America Securities
Okay. Yeah
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
... the floor system. I would say, pretty separate those, two just product categories.
George Staphos
Managing Director, Bank of America Securities
Yeah.
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Again, I-joist do have a role in terms of, again, creating that simplicity and that speed at the job site, and that's important to the builder. Always has been and certainly is today. I think that's, gonna be favorable relative to other options that are out there.
George Staphos
Managing Director, Bank of America Securities
Thanks, Nate.
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Yep.
George Staphos
Managing Director, Bank of America Securities
Kelly, you called out Oakdale, and I think it's kind of a $7 million impact in the quarter coming up. Is there any residual effect that we should build into the model? Then relatedly, we appreciate it. You qualitatively called out, hey, it's a little bit tougher start to the Q1 from weather than would normally be the case for weather in the Q1. Is there any sort of number you would sort of give us, hey, this has been the effect above and beyond a normal Q1? Anything that we could do to size our models. Then really my last question, and again, appreciate all the color. Where's your inventory position right now, in BMD relative to where you'd like it to be?
Kelly Hibbs
CFO and Treasurer, Boise Cascade
Yeah. Sure, George. Yeah, on the Q1 indicators, I would point you towards the table there in terms of, the volume and price expectations for Wood Products. For BMD, yeah, the sales pace is really going to matter. That's very important, and that will very much have an impact on how we close out the quarter. We've had multiple locations with multiple down days, even several locations this week were down because of some very tough weather. Yeah, it's created some challenges for us. Oakdale, that's. We've been working that project for some time now.
As expected, that facility is down and will be down for the entirety of this quarter.
George Staphos
Managing Director, Bank of America Securities
Mm-hmm
Kelly Hibbs
CFO and Treasurer, Boise Cascade
As we do that significant modernization project that we're excited to do. Again, that's a big important veneer supplier to our Alexandria, Louisiana, EWP mill. Yeah, we will, lose some volume from that and certainly that will give us some negative sequential cost impacts. Again, it was part of the plan, and we're on schedule, and then we'll see probably some of that continue into Q2 because, we'll be running at 50%-ish in Q2 as we work towards-
George Staphos
Managing Director, Bank of America Securities
Right
Kelly Hibbs
CFO and Treasurer, Boise Cascade
... completion of those projects by the end of Q2. I think inventory position, I'll send that one over to Mr. Strom.
Jeff Strom
COO, Boise Cascade
Hey, George, it's Jeff. On our inventory position overall-
George Staphos
Managing Director, Bank of America Securities
Hey
Jeff Strom
COO, Boise Cascade
You know what? I feel pretty good. Right now with all the uncertainty and lack of clarity out there, people are pulling more and more material from warehouse. Talking to our dealers, years I've been doing this, I've never heard so much conversation from that level about net working capital and days on hand. There is a real reliance, and we're sitting there ready to serve every single day.
George Staphos
Managing Director, Bank of America Securities
Okay. No doubt. Thank you, guys. I'll turn it over.
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Thanks, George.
George Staphos
Managing Director, Bank of America Securities
Good luck in the quarter.

Thank you.

Ketan Mamtora
Director of Building Products Equity Research, BMO Capital Markets
Good morning, and thanks for taking my question. Maybe to start with, on the BMD side, you have the slide where you look at sort of the last five years EBITDA margins. Clearly the operating environment, in 2024 and certainly looks like the start of this year is tougher, probably below normalized levels. Would you say given what you guys have done over the last few years in terms of the product mix, that you can say that, sort of cross-cycle margins in BMD are sort of, a little bit above 5%? Is that, would that be sort of a fair characterization?
Kelly Hibbs
CFO and Treasurer, Boise Cascade
Yeah. Our expectation and our strategy with the investments we've made and with the product mix shifts that we've made is that, BMD's margin is, through a cycle is in the mid-fives. We've demonstrated that. Now we could have periods like, for example, here in Q1 with the challenges on the top line, we may not hit 5% here in Q1 because of this pretty significant erosion here in the sales pace in Q1. Yes, over time, absolutely the strategy is we're mid-fives.
Ketan Mamtora
Director of Building Products Equity Research, BMO Capital Markets
Understood. Got it. Then, curious as you look at sort of your M&A pipeline, is that something that would be, sort of an area of interest as, seller expectations moderate either on the distribution side or, on the Wood Products side? Then just related to that, are there any other product categories within distribution that you think would make sense for you guys?
Kelly Hibbs

Yeah. On the M&A front, Ketan, the short answer is yes, we would have interest if it aligns with our strategy. I would say there's probably more potential opportunity on the distribution side than there would be on the Wood Products side. I think as we've talked before, we're very fortunate to be aligned with a lot of really world-class suppliers. Oftentimes, they're continuing to add products to their SKU set, and we get some natural growth, organic growth opportunity from there.
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Hey, Ketan, it's Nate. What are they experiencing? Where are there opportunities where Boise Cascade can step in? We try to have that same conversation with the suppliers as Kelly described. That's been an important part of our growth story, and I think we'll continue as we move forward.
Ketan Mamtora
Director of Building Products Equity Research, BMO Capital Markets
Got it. That's very helpful. I'll jump back in the queue. Good luck.
Kelly Hibbs
CFO and Treasurer, Boise Cascade
Thanks.
Nate Jorgensen
CEO, Boise Cascade
Thank you.

Nate Jorgensen

Great. Thank you. I appreciate everyone's time on the call today, and interest in Boise Cascade, and we'll look forward to getting caught up with this team here at the end of Q1. Again, thank you, and have a great day.
